passage:
In the government school at Nandgaon, Madam asked Tanuja to read the Hindi lesson aloud. Tanuja stood up, and the words on the page seemed to jump. "The farmer... the far... the fra..." Someone giggled. Tanuja crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a deep voice, "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!" The whole class burst out laughing, and so did she. Madam smiled but didn't move on to the next reader.
After the bell, Madam called her over. "You made them laugh very well. Was the reading hard today?" Tanuja shrugged and pulled another face. Her friend Zeenat, waiting by the door, noticed Tanuja's fingers twisting the end of her plait.

qa.q: What did Tanuja say in a deep voice?
qa.a: "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!"

qa.q: Why did Tanuja pull a funny face instead of trying the word again?
qa.a: She was embarrassed as the words jumped and someone giggled; the joke let her take charge so the class laughed with her, not at her.

qa.q: What choice did Madam make after the bell, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She praised the joke but gently asked if the reading was hard, which looks past the clowning to the worry underneath.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have understood from Tanuja's twisting fingers?
qa.a: Zeenat may have sensed that Tanuja was more worried than her funny faces showed.

grounding: A girl who stumbles while reading aloud turns it into a joke so the class laughs with her, while small signs show her worry.

passage:
In Year 5 at a primary school in Leeds, Bilal was halfway through his book report when he said "volcano" as "vol-CAN-o". Marek sniggered. Bilal froze for a second. Then he threw his arms up, wobbled like an erupting mountain and shouted, "KA-BOOM! Vol-CAN-o has exploded!" Everyone laughed, even Mrs Hughes. Bilal grinned and finished the report in a silly voice.
At lunch he did it again for the table, and again in the queue for the bus. At home, though, he asked his mum to listen to him read the report five times, until he could say every word right.

qa.q: Which word did Bilal say wrongly?
qa.a: "Volcano", as "vol-CAN-o".

qa.q: What does Bilal reading the report five times at home suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was worried and embarrassed about the mistake, even though his joke made it look as if he didn't care.

qa.q: What could Mrs Hughes try the next time Bilal reads aloud?
qa.a: Enjoy his humour, but offer a quiet practice run beforehand, so he doesn't need a joke to escape the worry. 🙂

qa.q: How might Marek feel after the snigger turned into the whole class laughing with Bilal?
qa.a: Marek may have felt the moment slip away, since the joke turned the laughter from mocking into sharing.

grounding: A boy in England turns a reading slip into a clowning act that gets the class laughing with him, but practises anxiously at home.

passage:
During the Class 6 spelling bee in the school hall, Alka misspelled "necessary" in front of two hundred students. She paused, then pretended to faint across the stage. The hall roared. Even the principal laughed.
For the rest of the week Alka joked through everything. She wore her tie as a headband in maths, answered science questions in a robot voice, and pulled faces whenever a teacher looked her way. Her class teacher, Jasleen Ma'am, noticed she hadn't handed in homework since the bee. On Friday she kept Alka back for a minute. "You're the funniest person in this class," she said. "And I think you might also be worried about something. Want to tell me?"
Alka stopped smiling. "I always get spellings wrong," she said quietly.

qa.q: Which word did Alka misspell at the spelling bee?
qa.a: "Necessary".

qa.q: Why might Alka have joked through everything for the rest of the week?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried about her spelling, and constant clowning kept everyone laughing so nobody saw the worry.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen Ma'am make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She praised Alka's humour and then gently named that she might be worried, which made it safe for Alka to admit the real problem.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen Alka's faint?
qa.a: As a hilarious bit of fun, probably without guessing she was embarrassed underneath.

grounding: After a spelling-bee mistake a girl clowns constantly, and a teacher notices the joking hides a worry.

passage:
I'm Gurpreet, and I sit behind Madhuri in Class 4. On Monday Miss asked her to read the recipe in our English book. At "ingredients" she said "in-GREE-dee-ents" and a couple of kids snickered. Madhuri stopped, put on a posh voice like a TV cook, waved her ruler like a spoon and said, "Today, darlings, we cook the in-GREE-dee-ents!" The whole class cracked up. Even Miss smiled.
She's always funny. But she does it every single time it's her turn to read. On reading days she chews her pencil flat and asks to go to the washroom before English. Maybe she just likes making us laugh. Or maybe she'd rather we laugh at the joke than at her.

qa.q: Which word did Madhuri stumble on?
qa.a: "Ingredients"; she said "in-GREE-dee-ents".

qa.q: Why might Madhuri turn the mistake into a TV-cook act?
qa.a: The joke lets her take control of the moment so the class laughs with her, not at her, hiding embarrassment and maybe worry about reading.

qa.q: How could Miss support Madhuri after noticing the pattern?
qa.a: Miss could quietly check whether reading aloud is hard for Madhuri and offer practice or a heads-up before her turn, while still enjoying her humour.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the jokes differently from the rest of the class?
qa.a: Gurpreet enjoys them too, but notices the chewed pencil and washroom trips on reading days, so the jokes look like they might be covering worry.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a child who stumbles while reading and turns it into a silly act that gets the class laughing with her, with signs of hidden worry.

passage:
Monday. In science, Hafsa, ten, read "photosynthesis" as "photo-sin-thesis". Someone giggled. She held up an invisible camera and said, "Say cheese, everyone, it's photo-sin time!" The class roared, and her ears stopped burning.
Wednesday. It was her turn again. Before she even started, she crossed her eyes and made a fish face. Everyone laughed, waiting for more. "Hafsa, just read, please," said the teacher. That evening she shoved her reading book under the bed. "I'm the funny one, Noor baji," she told her cousin. "Not the reading one."
Saturday. Noor baji sat with her on the floor. They clapped out hard words together: pho-to-syn-the-sis. Hafsa still made jokes, silly ones about plants eating sunshine. But she read the whole next page, stopping only twice.

qa.q: How did Hafsa read "photosynthesis" on Monday?
qa.a: As "photo-sin-thesis".

qa.q: What does "I'm the funny one, not the reading one" reveal about Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: It reveals she worries she is bad at reading, and being funny feels like a safer thing to be known for.

qa.q: What choice by Noor baji on Saturday helped?
qa.a: Practising hard words with Hafsa by clapping out the syllables, without taking her jokes away, so reading felt less scary 🙂

qa.q: What might the teacher be thinking when saying, "Hafsa, just read, please"?
qa.a: The teacher may think Hafsa is just being silly on purpose, without seeing the worry about reading underneath the fish face.

grounding: Illustrates a child who covers reading stumbles with jokes that make the class laugh with her, while the clowning hides a worry that shows at home.

passage:
Dear diary, it's Sharmila.

Today in science Miss asked me to read the paragraph about plants. I got stuck on "photosynthesis." I said "photo-sin-thesis" and someone giggled. My face went HOT. So I made a fish face, puffed my cheeks and said, "Photo-fishy-thesis!" Everybody laughed, even Miss a little. Parul laughed so much she snorted.

It felt good. Like I was in charge of the laughing, not them.

But now it's bedtime and my tummy feels tight. Tomorrow is reading again. I don't want to make a fish face every day.

I think I'll ask Amma to practise the hard words with me tonight. Just a few.

qa.q: Which word did Sharmila get stuck on?
qa.a: "Photosynthesis."

qa.q: Why did Sharmila make a fish face after stumbling?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed when someone giggled, and turning it into a joke felt like taking control of the laughing.

qa.q: What small step is Sharmila planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Practising the hard words with Amma, which tackles the reading worry underneath instead of relying on jokes.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt laughing at the fish face?
qa.a: Parul probably felt amused and happy, not realising Sharmila was covering embarrassment.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles while reading making a silly face to get the class laughing along, though the clowning covers a worry.

passage: In the village school near Bathinda, the teacher asked Baljeet to read the Punjabi poem aloud. He got the first line wrong, then the second. He stopped. Then he clutched his heart, rolled his eyes and fell dramatically sideways off the bench. "The poem has defeated me!" The whole class roared. Nitin, beside him, laughed until he cried. Even the teacher smiled. But she'd noticed something. Baljeet always did a funny act when it was his turn to read: a sneeze, a voice, a faint. Never when it was maths or games. After class she called him over. "You're very funny. Is reading hard for you?" Baljeet's grin slipped for a second. "No, Ma'am." Then, quietly, "A bit." She nodded. "Stay for ten minutes on Thursdays. Just you and me."

qa.q: What did Baljeet do after getting the second line wrong?
qa.a: He clutched his heart, rolled his eyes and fell dramatically sideways off the bench.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet always do a funny act when it's his turn to read?
qa.a: Reading makes him feel anxious and embarrassed, and making the class laugh lets him stay in control instead of showing he's struggling.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that could help Baljeet most?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern, gently asked about reading privately, and offered extra time on Thursdays.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Baljeet's performances?
qa.a: Nitin probably sees them as hilarious and doesn't guess they hide worry about reading.

grounding: Shows a child who stumbles reading aloud clowning to get the class laughing with him, while the teacher notices the worry beneath.

passage: In the classroom in São Paulo, Paulo stood to read his history paragraph and tripped over "independence." He tried again. "Indepen... indep..." Someone at the back snorted. Paulo froze, then switched to a robot voice. "ERROR. WORD. TOO. LONG. REBOOTING." The class exploded with laughter. Alejandro nearly fell off his chair. Paulo sat down grinning and took a bow. At break, Alejandro was still laughing. "You're so funny, man. You always do that." Paulo kicked at the ground. "Yeah." "Wait, do you do it on purpose?" Paulo was quiet. "When I get stuck, everyone's looking. If I make them laugh, it's like I chose it." Alejandro stopped laughing. "Oh." Paulo shrugged. "Doesn't matter." But he didn't do the robot for the rest of the day.

qa.q: Which word did Paulo trip over?
qa.a: "Independence."

qa.q: Why did Paulo switch to a robot voice?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed with everyone looking, and making them laugh felt like he had chosen the moment instead of failing at it.

qa.q: How could Alejandro support Paulo now that he knows?
qa.a: Alejandro could avoid pushing him to be funny when reading, and maybe practise hard words with him or suggest he talk to the teacher.

qa.q: What changes for Alejandro after Paulo explains?
qa.a: Alejandro stops laughing, seeing that the jokes cover worry, not just fun.

grounding: Shows a child stumbling while reading and using a silly voice to get the class laughing with him, with the clowning hiding worry.

passage:
When Rafiq's turn came to read aloud in Class 4, he stumbled on "mysterious". "Mys... mister... mystery-ous?" Somebody at the back snorted.

Before the snort could grow, Rafiq crossed his eyes, puffed out his cheeks and said in a robot voice, "MY-STER-I-OUS. Word defeated me. Rafiq shutting down." The whole class burst out laughing, and he grinned and bowed.

His friend Imran laughed hardest. But at lunch Imran noticed Rafiq quietly practising the next page under the desk, lips moving, finger on each word.

"You're doing the robot tomorrow too?" Imran asked.

"Only if I get stuck," Rafiq said, not looking up. "I always get stuck."

qa.q: Which word did Rafiq stumble on?
qa.a: Rafiq stumbled on "mysterious".

qa.q: Why did Rafiq make the robot face so quickly?
qa.a: Rafiq felt embarrassed when someone snorted, and turning it into a joke let him control the laughter so the class laughed with him, not at him.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Rafiq?
qa.a: The teacher could let Rafiq practise the passage beforehand or read in a small group, so reading feels less risky and the joke isn't the only shield.

qa.q: How does Imran see Rafiq's joke by lunchtime?
qa.a: Imran laughed at first but then glimpses the worry behind it, seeing Rafiq practise and hearing "I always get stuck."

grounding: Shows a boy who stumbles over a word and turns it into a robot act so the class laughs with him, while worry sits underneath.

passage:
Monday: Jagdish tripped over "photograph" in English reading, said "foto-graaf", then stuck out his tongue and wobbled his head. The class roared. Ishita, beside him, laughed too.

Wednesday: he got stuck again, on "Wednesday" itself, and this time did a whole dance, flapping his arms like a hen. Even Ms Rego smiled. Ishita noticed his ears had gone red before the dance, not after.

Friday: when Ms Rego called his name, Jagdish started the hen dance before reading a single word. Ms Rego said gently, "Just try the first line, Jagdish. No show needed." The room went quiet. He read slowly, stumbled once, and kept going.

At break he asked Ishita, "Was that boring?"

"No," she said. "It was brave."

qa.q: Which word did Jagdish get stuck on on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jagdish got stuck on "Wednesday" itself.

qa.q: What might Jagdish's red ears before the hen dance suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Jagdish was embarrassed and worried about stumbling, and the joke was a way to take control of the moment.

qa.q: What did Ms Rego's Friday words get right?
qa.a: She kindly removed the need for a show, letting Jagdish try the line without the class watching a performance, so he could face the worry.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Jagdish by Friday?
qa.a: Ishita sees past the clowning to the nerves, and calls his plain reading brave.

grounding: Over a week a boy clowns every time he stumbles while reading, until his teacher lets him read without needing the show.

passage:
Lokesh, you think your Dada was always serious? When I was ten, in Meerut, our Hindi teacher Pandey-ji made each boy read aloud. I couldn't read fast. The letters seemed to jump about. So the first time I stumbled, I pulled my ears like a donkey and brayed. The whole class fell over laughing, and Pandey-ji laughed too.

After that I did it every time. Donkey, monkey, a crying baby. I was the funniest boy in school. Nobody knew I went home each day with my stomach in knots before reading class.

Then one day Pandey-ji kept me back and said, "Vikas, your donkey is very good. Now, can you read me this line without him?" Every afternoon for a month I read to him alone. Slowly the letters stopped jumping so much. And I didn't need the donkey any more.

qa.q: Which animal did young Vikas imitate the first time he stumbled?
qa.a: Young Vikas pulled his ears like a donkey and brayed.

qa.q: Why did young Vikas keep clowning every time?
qa.a: Young Vikas felt anxious and embarrassed about reading slowly, with a knotted stomach each day, and the jokes kept that worry hidden.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Vikas stop needing the donkey?
qa.a: Pandey-ji praised the donkey but asked for a line without it, then gave a month of private reading practice.

qa.q: How might Pandey-ji have seen young Vikas's clowning?
qa.a: Pandey-ji enjoyed it but seemed to sense worry behind it, and chose quiet practice instead of scolding.

grounding: A grandfather recalls clowning whenever he stumbled over reading as a boy, and how that hid a daily worry.

passage: The power went off during the monsoon reading lesson, and Ramesh sir asked Sarika to read aloud by the light from the window. She stumbled on "environment", then on "enormous". A boy at the back snickered. Quick as anything, Sarika crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a robot voice, "Sarika has stopped working! Please restart!" The class burst out laughing, with her this time. Ramesh sir smiled too. But at break he noticed Sarika sitting alone, picking at her tiffin. "That was funny," he said. "Is reading aloud hard for you?" She shrugged, then nodded, very small. "Every time." He said they could practise together at lunch, just the two of them.

qa.q: Which two words did Sarika stumble on?
qa.a: "Environment" and "enormous".

qa.q: Why did Sarika do the robot act?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed after stumbling and hearing the snicker; the joke let her control the moment so the class laughed with her, not at her.

qa.q: What did Ramesh sir do that was wise?
qa.a: He noticed her alone at break, looked past the joke to ask whether reading aloud was hard, and offered private practice.

qa.q: How might the boy who snickered feel after the joke?
qa.a: He probably laughed along; the moment turned, and his snicker lost its sting.

grounding: A girl who stumbles while reading gets the class laughing with her, and a teacher sees the worry behind the clowning.

passage: In the week before Durga Puja, the Kolkata school buzzed with holiday plans. When Sumit's turn came to read the Bengali poem aloud, he tripped over a long word and his face went red. Then he stood up straight, bowed like a king, and said, "Thank you, thank you, I'll be here all week." Everyone laughed. The teacher shook her head, smiling. Sumit did it every time now: a joke, a face, a bow. His friend Sharmila noticed he never read more than two lines before joking. Walking home past the bamboo of the half-built pandal, she asked, "Do you joke because reading is hard?" Sumit kicked a pebble. "If they laugh at the joke, they don't laugh at me," he said.

qa.q: What did Sumit say after bowing?
qa.a: "Thank you, thank you, I'll be here all week."

qa.q: Why does Sumit joke every time he reads?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and worried about stumbling, and the joke keeps control, so they laugh at the joke and not at him.

qa.q: What could help Sumit beyond the jokes?
qa.a: Telling the teacher or a parent that reading aloud is hard, so he gets practice and support instead of always hiding it.

qa.q: What has Sharmila noticed?
qa.a: That Sumit never reads more than two lines before joking, so she senses the worry behind it.

grounding: A boy who stumbles reading aloud turns it into a joke every time, and a friend sees the worry it hides.

passage:
"How was school, Lavanya?"
"Great, Amma! I made the whole class laugh."
"Oh? How?"
"I was reading about the planets and I said a name wrong, so I pretended to be an alien. Everyone laughed."
"With you or at you?"
"With me. Because I did it first."
Her mother, Sharmila, put down the knife. "Do you do that a lot?"
"Kind of. Whenever I read."
"What happens if you don't make a joke?"
Lavanya went quiet. "Then they might laugh the other way."
"That sounds tiring, chellam."
"It is," Lavanya whispered. "Sometimes."
"Shall we read together tonight, under the winter blanket? No audience."
"Okay."

qa.q: What did Lavanya pretend to be?
qa.a: An alien.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's reply about them laughing the other way reveal?
qa.a: She is worried about being laughed at, and joking first protects her; it also makes her tired.

qa.q: What did Sharmila suggest?
qa.a: Reading together tonight under the blanket, with no audience, so Lavanya can practise without needing a joke.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel on learning Lavanya jokes every time she reads?
qa.a: Concerned and tender, sensing how tiring it is for her daughter.

grounding: A girl who stumbles when reading clowns so the class laughs with her, and her mother sees the worry beneath.

passage:
On Children's Day, Ma'am picked me to read the story aloud. I got to "magnificent" and it came out "mag-nif-nif-icent". My face went hot. So I crossed my eyes, stuck out my tongue and said, "Sonali has broken down, please restart." Everyone laughed, even Ma'am. Avni laughed so hard she snorted.
It felt good, like I was in charge again. But at lunch my tummy still felt tight.
I do the funny face a lot now. When I don't know an answer. When I'm scared to read. Sometimes I wish I could just say, "That word is hard for me."

qa.q: Which word did Sonali stumble on?
qa.a: "Magnificent".

qa.q: Why did Sonali make a silly face?
qa.a: Sonali felt embarrassed and hot-faced 😅, and getting everyone to laugh along felt like being in charge again instead of being laughed at.

qa.q: What could help Sonali in future?
qa.a: Quietly telling the teacher or a friend that some words are hard, and practising reading aloud at home, so the funny face is not needed every time.

qa.q: How does Avni see the moment?
qa.a: Avni just finds it hilarious, snorting with laughter, and probably does not notice Sonali's tight tummy or worry.

grounding: A child who stumbles while reading aloud clowns to get the class laughing, while the joking hides worry.
